Developed by VisiVault Analytics Ltd. · October 2026 · Management report
Prairie Auto Care Group is a FICTIONAL multi-location Calgary collision repair and car care business. Its business model (three Calgary locations with distinct roles, published hours, service menu, OEM-certified collision work, direct billing of insurers) is inspired by a public Calgary auto care group's website (retrieved 2026-10-09); every repair order, cost, technician, insurer, customer and financial figure is synthetic. No relationship with or endorsement by any real company is implied.

Important notice

This report analyses a fictional auto care group built on synthetic data to demonstrate VisiVault Analytics' capabilities. None of the operational or financial figures describe any real company. The analyses are designed to complement - not replace - a repair business's existing shop-management, insurance-estimating, parts-ordering and accounting systems.

3. Business challenges this platform addresses

  • Cycle time and promises: parts availability, insurer approvals and supplements push vehicles past their promised date - the strongest driver of customer satisfaction.
  • Technician capacity: collision demand peaks with snow and winter driving, tires peak twice a year, summer is quieter; labour is the largest controllable cost.
  • Job profitability: fixed customer-pay quotes, parts price changes, discounts and comebacks erode margin job by job - often invisible in monthly totals.
  • Insurer cash cycle: direct billing means most collision revenue is collected weeks after delivery; documentation quality drives payment speed.
  • Multi-branch economics: work moves between branches (e.g. a concierge site sending collision repairs to the main shop); fair branch results need transfer pricing, eliminations and transparent overhead allocation.

Six models: revenue, RO volume / billed-hours demand, repair cycle time (best: Ridge regression, MAE 6.1 days vs 6.5 for the baseline), parts demand, technician capacity and expected cash collections. Each is compared against a simple baseline with time-based validation. Model performance on synthetic data does not establish real-world prediction accuracy.

Collision and mechanical revenue are capacity-constrained in the forecast: a 10% efficiency gain changes revenue by only $24,237 because demand - not technician capacity - limits sales most months; the gain shows up as lower overtime.

1. Price and quote review for jobs that do not cover shop overhead; teardown before fixed customer-pay quotes

Estimate: operating profit $142,328, cash $128,095 (12 months). How calculated: 1736 ROs (16%) fell $355,820 short of direct cost + shop overhead ($88 per clocked hour) in 12 months; largest gaps: Interior & exterior detailing ($282,249), Paintless dent repair ($21,755), Paint protection (film, ceramic coating) ($10,680). Assume 40% recovered through minimum charges, package pricing and quote discipline. Assumptions: Customers accept minimum labour charges / revised quotes; goodwill discounts approved by the branch manager only. KPIs: Fully loaded profit per RO, unprofitable RO count, estimate-to-actual labour variance

2. Grow detailing & paint protection at SE Concierge (insurer-referral and dealer packages)

Estimate: operating profit $187,364, cash $161,876 (12 months). How calculated: Engine re-run with detailing & other services +25% (with installer labour). Assumptions: Demand exists at current prices; installer capacity added in line with volume. KPIs: SE revenue, SE contribution, PPF backlog days

3. Preferred-supplier agreement and monthly price audit on the top OEM / aftermarket suppliers

Estimate: operating profit $163,169, cash $133,809 (12 months). How calculated: Special-order parts are ~82% of parts spend. Engine re-run with parts cost -3%. Assumptions: Volume rebate or discount of 3% on special-order parts; no change in quality or lead time. KPIs: Parts margin %, price variance vs estimate

4. Flat-rate incentive and training to lift efficiency - paired with demand growth

Estimate: operating profit $34,017, cash $16,193 (12 months). How calculated: Engine re-run with efficiency +10%: only $24,237 extra revenue because collision demand rarely exceeds capacity; the benefit is mainly lower overtime. Efficiency pays off when combined with volume growth. Assumptions: Demand-constrained most months; capacity binds only in winter peaks. KPIs: Efficiency, overtime %, productivity

5. Seasonal, service-level reorder points for stocked parts (tires, oil, filters, brakes)

Estimate: operating profit $13,048, cash $13,048 (12 months). How calculated: 1,306 emergency (stockout) orders in 12 months, $202,961 bought at a ~12% premium ($21,746). 121 branch-SKUs need a higher seasonal reorder point. Assume 60% of the premium avoided. Assumptions: Reorder points from reorder_point_recommendations.csv (95/90/85% service by ABC class); weekly review kept. KPIs: Fill rate, emergency orders, inventory turnover, aged stock

6. Pre-delivery QC checklist and comeback root-cause review (lifetime warranty)

Estimate: operating profit $7,802, cash $7,802 (12 months). How calculated: Warranty comebacks cost $22,291 in parts & labour over 12 months (1.5% of ROs). Assume 35% fewer comebacks. Assumptions: Comeback rates compared with the expected rate for each technician's job mix (no raw ranking). KPIs: Comeback rate, rework cost, CSAT

7. Parts-first scheduling with daily supplier escalation for collision jobs

Estimate: operating profit $5,297, cash $20,408 (12 months). How calculated: Parts waiting averages 9.5 days per collision job vs 1.8 days waiting for a technician. Weakest on-time suppliers: Import Specialty Parts (fictional) (43%), Westline Glass Distribution (fictional) (46%). Engine re-run with cycle time -15% (less work in progress, fewer waiting customers lost). Assumptions: Vehicles dropped off only when parts are confirmed; backorders escalated within 24 h; alternative certified parts approved faster. KPIs: Keys-to-keys days, parts waiting days, on-time vs original promise, CSAT

8. Same-day electronic invoicing with complete photo & supplement files; weekly follow-up of items past terms

Estimate: operating profit $0, cash $122,626 (12 months). How calculated: Insurer receivables $573,561 at 30-Sep-2026; average payment 27 days (non-DRP insurers slower: 38 days). Engine re-run with collection delays -20%. Assumptions: Most delay is documentation and follow-up, not insurer policy; fictional insurers only. KPIs: Insurer DSO, receivables > 60 days, short-pays

10. Implementation requirements

  • Read-only exports (CSV / API / scheduled reports) from the shop-management system: repair orders with status history, technician time clock, parts lines.
  • Estimating and insurer data already exchanged with insurers: estimates, supplements, approvals; invoice and payment remittances.
  • Accounting: monthly trial balance / GL, AR and AP ageing; payroll summary by branch; fixed-asset register.
  • A named data contact (2-3 h/week) and a monthly 60-minute management review.

11. Risk considerations

  • Data quality: clock-on discipline and RO status timestamps vary; the diagnostic measures completeness before any KPI is published.
  • Fairness: technician metrics are mix- and role-adjusted and shown with evidence levels; they support coaching, not discipline.
  • Privacy & security: customer personal information is excluded or pseudonymised; data stays in Canada (PIPEDA / Alberta PIPA); read-only access.
  • Model risk: forecasts are re-validated on real history before use; scenario results are decision aids, not guarantees.
  • Insurer relationships: claim analytics are for internal process improvement; no insurer is characterised publicly.
